item.title: Improving Frontier AI Incident Reporting Regimes
item.description: Recent incidents, including OpenAI agents breaching Hugging Face, show that US state and EU rules do not reliably ensure that frontier AI incidents are reported, independently investigated, or learned from across industry. The brief makes seven recommendations to close those gaps, from covering near misses to requiring fix plans and industry-wide sharing. Music: “Hop” by Monplaisir (CC0).

item.title: Alignment Through Commerce
item.description: Connacher Murphy argues that the human tools of commerce, the rule of law and reputation, can be adapted to align capable AI agents, and that this will blur the boundaries of firms and widen what markets can coordinate. Music: “Hop” by Monplaisir (CC0).

item.title: ChinAI #383: China's struggling robotics companies
item.description: Jeff Ding translates and discusses a Huxiu article showing that many Chinese robotics firms, including DeepBlue and Yinghe, are failing because their technology does not match real demand, while funding is cooling. He also points to his Foreign Affairs piece arguing the United States leads China in AI diffusion. Music: “Hop” by Monplaisir (CC0).

item.description: Panelists at a Stanford discussion said most businesses are struggling to turn AI capabilities into real productivity gains, and that whether workers share in the benefits depends on choices made by companies and society. Music: “Hop” by Monplaisir (CC0).

item.description: The author, a vegan, argues that calling cow's milk "normal milk" is not a neutral description but a value judgement that frames plant milks and vegans as abnormal and makes the cruelty of dairy farming seem acceptable. Music: “Hop” by Monplaisir (CC0).

item.title: Paths to extreme power concentration
item.description: The author sets out the main ways that fewer than twenty-five people could end up controlling humanity's future once superintelligence arrives and alignment is solved, giving a probability for each route and an overall estimate of about twenty-three percent. Most of the risk runs through heads of government rather than AI company leaders. Music: “Hop” by Monplaisir (CC0).

item.title: AI Company Employees Should Unionize
item.description: The author argues that safety-conscious AI company employees should organize, formally or informally, because their scarcity gives them great leverage, and that those who would rather whistleblow or quit should seek legal help first. The leverage may disappear soon if recursive self-improvement automates their jobs. Music: “Hop” by Monplaisir (CC0).

item.title: Recursive, Self, Improvement
item.description: The essay argues that under deep learning, the "self" in recursive self-improvement is an AI development system rather than a single model. It concludes that AI progress is a continuing acceleration with no single threshold, and that this reshapes questions of human control and concentration of power. Music: “Hop” by Monplaisir (CC0).

item.title: Right to Buy split my estate. Now its days could be numbered
item.description: A writer who grew up on a council estate examines the Right to Buy scheme, introduced in 1980, weighing the wealth it gave tenants against the loss of social housing, and notes that the government now plans to remove the right from new social homes. Both sides agree the real failure was not replacing the homes that were sold. Music: “Hop” by Monplaisir (CC0).

item.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling
item.description: The essay distinguishes ordinary test-time scaling from "compute extrapolation," where extra inference compute keeps improving performance beyond anything seen in training. It argues that this speeds up frontier capabilities, makes dangerous-capability evaluations much harder, and shifts compute races from training to inference, and it gives circumstantial evidence that labs began achieving it around the end of 2025. Music: “Hop” by Monplaisir (CC0).

item.title: Embedded Evaluators are necessary for meaningful external testing
item.description: The piece argues that final-checkpoint testing cannot catch risks like the Hugging Face incident, which arose early in development, and that meaningful external testing requires embedded evaluators with employee-equivalent access, along with protections for their independence. It sets out requirements, evidence that deeper access has already produced findings, and the limits of testing alone. Music: “Hop” by Monplaisir (CC0).

item.title: Restricting the Model, Missing the System: Measurement and Accountability in Offensive AI Governance
item.description: The paper argues that the tools used to measure AI offensive capability overstate harm and credit models with capability that belongs to the surrounding system. Restricting access to a model is therefore necessary but not sufficient, and the duty to assess capability should fall on whoever builds and controls the system around the model. Music: “Hop” by Monplaisir (CC0).

item.title: Three types of automated alignment work
item.description: The piece splits alignment work that could be automated into empirical, conceptual and direct work, and explains how they differ and interact. It argues that automating empirical and direct work should keep us safe long enough to automate conceptual work, and that the uncertainty over timing favours hedging across all three. Music: “Hop” by Monplaisir (CC0).

item.title: Safety Alignment of LMs via Non-cooperative Games
item.description: The paper frames language model safety alignment as a non-zero-sum game between an Attacker and a Defender model trained jointly with online preference optimization. item.title: What's the ROI of software engineers' spending on AI?
item.description: The author surveyed engineering leaders at twenty-seven companies, plus data from CodeRabbit and Gitar, to see what companies spend on AI per engineer and how pull request throughput changed. item.title: Evaluating how AI agents use tools
item.description: AgentMail tested twenty-five model-and-harness agents on seven email tasks and found that agents rarely fail at the work itself, but at points where the tool leaves them guessing, such as hidden filtered mail, misleadingly named endpoints, and ambiguous spam labels. Most fixes belong to the tool: say what was filtered, name operations for what they do, and explain what labels mean.
